The plasma-spray coating process uses an ionized gas plasma to melt and propel powdered coating alloy toward the substrate.
Low pressure plasma spray (LPPS) is used to apply the metallic bond coating layer to improve oxidation resistance and bond strength compared to conventional air plasma spray.
Plasma-sprayed TBC systems incorporate 10-15% porosity and partially stabilized zirconia compositions to provide strain accommodation.
Thermal cycling is required to fully develop the subcritical microcracking in plasma-sprayed yttria-stabilized zirconia coatings.
EB-PVD TBC systems achieve a strain-tolerant columnar microstructure in the zirconia ceramic layer.
EB-PVD TBC systems require a smooth, preferably polished, surface for optimal adhesion through a chemical bond.
Toughness values for plasma-sprayed and EB-PVD TBC systems range from 0.5 to 3.2 MPa√m.
Zirconia spalling can be caused by both tensile and compressive strains in the TBC system.
Denser zirconia coatings, such as laser-glazed EB-PVD, exhibit better erosion resistance than more porous plasma-sprayed coatings.
The durability of a TBC system depends on the strain tolerance, interface toughness, and oxidation resistance of the coating layers.
This program aims to develop thermomechanical and thermochemical life prediction models for plasma-sprayed and EB-PVD TBC systems.
The first year of the program focused on literature review, specimen procurement, and characterization of the TBC systems.
Thermomechanical and thermochemical testing of the TBC systems is ongoing to calibrate the life prediction models.
Eddy current technology has been demonstrated as a feasible method for nondestructively measuring zirconia layer thickness.
Factory engine tests will be used to validate the accuracy of the TBC life prediction models developed in this program.
